extracted.intended_audience: astronomers, geodesists, instrument-makers, and natural philosophers/readers of the Philosophical Transactions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and methodological standards for dividing instrument limbs (quadrants) into equal angular parts and for measuring the Earth's meridian by long-baseline triangulation and astronomical observation. Contains trig procedures, instrument‑choice recommendations, timekeeping/observation protocol, and related practical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Division of the Arc on the Limb of a Quadrant, or other such like Instrument, by Concentric Circles, and a right Diagonal Line
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure for dividing the breadth of an instrument's limb into equal angular parts by drawing concentric circles and using a rectilineal diagonal line intersecting them; given the inner radius r, the outer radius z, and the contained angle A, compute the transverse segment lengths a, b, c, ... so that the transverse intersections determine equal angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives the trig relations: with the breadth RL = /, AR = r, AZ = z = / + r, and angle RAZ = A to be divided into n equal parts by right lines a, b, c, etc. Details how to find angles p, q, etc. (z + r : z - r :: tang. t±l : tang. ^; and ^ + ^ = /j). Then knowing angles and side r, use sin relations (sin a : r :: sin p : a) to find a, b, c, etc. Worked numerical examples provided (e.g., r = 1, / = 0.2, z = 1.2, A = 10') with tables of sines and computed radii. Includes complete worked numeric procedure and an alternative calculation using convenient choices for intermediate angles to simplify divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidelines for dividing broad vs narrow instrument limbs (error considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the limb of an instrument is broad relative to the radius, dividing by concentric circles and diagonal lines can introduce small or larger errors; when limbs are narrow (as in very large instruments) the resulting differences are insensible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes two illustrative cases: limb breadth equal to the 5th part or the 10th part of the shorter radius with the angle to be divided 10' — accuracy then depends on the common trigonometrical canon and last digits may be ambiguous. If the limb breadth is the 30th or 40th (or smaller) part of the radius and the angle to be divided is 10'' or less, differences are smaller than can be shown by common trigonometric tables and become insensible; concentric circles will appear equidistant to the senses. Also: errors on broad limbs of smaller instruments may be measurable, but on large instruments with narrow limbs errors are negligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Normalization of radius to 1 for trigonometric computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical recommendation to take the shorter radius r = 1 for computations instead of large integer radii, to save multiplications/divisions and keep sines in decimal parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author states he commonly sets r = 1 (not 10,000,000 as others do) so that all multiplications and divisions by the radius are saved; sines become decimal parts and, when necessary, ciphers are prefixed to occupy integer places. This simplifies tabulation and arithmetic in the examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing a convenient intermediate angle to simplify calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice to select an intermediate angle (p) of convenient magnitude, determinable by exact minutes (avoiding seconds/thirds), to simplify finding radii for the divisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of using minute/second/third-level angles arising from exact geometry, choose p such that it is expressible in exact minutes; then the tabular sine can be used and the length of the greatest radius z and intermediate radii can be obtained by a single division. Example: taking A = 10' and selecting p = 178° 10' (supplement 1°50') yields tabular sines convenient to compute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meridian measurement methodology (Picard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards and methods for determining the length of a degree of the Earth's meridian by measuring a long straight baseline and constructing a series of triangulation triangles with accurate angular observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommendations and practices used by Picard: choose and measure a very long straight basis (5663 toises in his work — much longer than prior ~1000 toise bases); use pikes joined by screws and stakes to mark the base; employ accurate instruments with telescopic sights (quadrant of 38 inches radius with telescopic sights, and instruments whose limb was an arch of 1/4 circle with 10-foot radius) instead of common sights; form a series of triangles (13 in his chain) and compute sides from measured angles; measure angles of declination to the meridian from chosen stations; sum computed meridian segments to obtain toises per degree (Picard found ~57060 toises per degree). Notes that the polygonal approximation differs from the true curve by only about 3 feet per degree — an acceptably small error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instrument choice and observational practice for high accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for instrument selection and observational technique to improve accuracy of geodetic and astronomical measurements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use telescopic sights rather than common sights for taking angular positions; use large instruments (larger radius limbs) with narrow limb breadth to reduce division errors; employ pendulum-based timekeeping and adjust/verify watches (e.g., pendulum watches were adjusted by the sun the same day and verified the next day); select straight, plain grounds for long baselines; mark and measure with standardized pikes/stakes; and use telescopical sights for angle-taking in triangulation and for measuring minutes/seconds in the heavens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pendulum-based standardization and proposal for universal measure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a seconds pendulum as a standard length and proposal to derive a universal foot/toise/perch/mile from the pendulum length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Picard notes a pendulum vibrating a second (computed by mean solar motion) is 36 inches and 8 1/2 lines of Paris measure; he suggests making this pendulum the astronomical radius, one quarter of which could be the universal foot, double that the universal toise/fathom (with stated ratios to Parisian toise), quadruple the radius the universal perch, and 1000 such perches the universal mile. He conjectures the pendulum length is consistent across latitudes and could serve as a universal standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lunar eclipse observation and timekeeping protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for timing and reporting lunar eclipse observations to ensure precise, comparable records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record the beginning of penumbra, immersion (true shadow ingress), total immersion, emersion, and end times with precise timekeeping; measure the moon's diameter before the eclipse; use large pendulum watches adjusted by the sun the same day and verified the next day; note auxiliary reference (e.g., star altitudes such as Capella at a specified time) to check instrument alignment and timing. Multiple observers (Flamsteed, Bulliald, Cassini, Picard, Roemer, etc.) coordinate times and compare observed times with tabular predictions (Flamsteed's tables) for verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical agricultural timing by lunar phase (Munting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guideline for sowing/setting seeds based on moon increase/decrease depending on whether the plant bears fruit above or below ground.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: kernels and seeds of trees and plants that bear fruit above ground should be set or sown in the decrease of the moon; those that bear fruit under ground (turnips, parsnips, carrots, etc.) should be committed to the ground in the increase of the moon. The author warns that doing the contrary tends to yield plants with many branches and large leaves but small fruit. Also gives grafting advice for apples to obtain large fruit (graft good grafts onto stocks produced from seed and deprived of their heart-root).
